Looking at this problem, I need to determine for which $r > 0$ the unit ball $B = \{f \in C([0,1]) : \|f\|_\infty \leq 1\}$ admits a finite $r$-dense subset under $d_{\sup}(f,g) = \|f - g\|_\infty$.

**Answer:** A finite $r$-dense subset exists if and only if $r > 1$.

## Proof

### Part 1: For $r > 1$, a finite $r$-dense subset exists.

Take $Y = \{0\}$ (the zero function). For any $f \in B$, we have $\|f - 0\|_\infty = \|f\|_\infty \leq 1 < r$. So $Y$ is $r$-dense. $\checkmark$

### Part 2: For $r \leq 1$, no finite $r$-dense subset exists.

We show that for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$, there exist $n$ functions in $B$ that are pairwise at distance exactly $2$. This forces any $r$-dense set (with $r \leq 1$) to have at least $n$ elements, so no finite set suffices.

**Construction.** Fix $n \geq 1$ and set $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2n}$. For $k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1$, define $t_k = \frac{k}{n}$ and:

$$f_k(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x \leq t_k, \\ -1 & \text{if } x \geq t_k + \varepsilon, \\ \text{linear on } [t_k,\, t_k+\varepsilon] & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$

Each $f_k$ is continuous with $\|f_k\|_\infty = 1$, so $f_k \in B$.

**Pairwise distance.** For $i < j$, we have $t_i + \varepsilon \leq t_i + \frac{1}{2n} \leq \frac{i}{n} + \frac{1}{2n} \leq \frac{i+1}{n} \leq t_j$ (since $j \geq i+1$). On the interval $[t_i + \varepsilon,\, t_j]$, we have $f_i = -1$ and $f_j = 1$, so:

$$\|f_i - f_j\|_\infty \geq |(-1) - 1| = 2.$$

Since both functions take values in $[-1, 1]$, we also have $\|f_i - f_j\|_\infty \leq 2$. Therefore $\|f_i - f_j\|_\infty = 2$ for all $i \neq j$.

**Packing argument.** Suppose $Y = \{g_1, \dots, g_m\}$ is $r$-dense with $r \leq 1$. For each $f_k$, there exists $g_{\sigma(k)} \in Y$ with $\|f_k - g_{\sigma(k)}\|_\infty < r$. If $\sigma(i) = \sigma(j) = \ell$ for some $i \neq j$, then by the triangle inequality:

$$2 = \|f_i - f_j\|_\infty \leq \|f_i - g_\ell\|_\infty + \|g_\ell - f_j\|_\infty < r + r = 2r \leq 2,$$

which gives $2 < 2$, a contradiction. Therefore $\sigma$ is injective, so $m \geq n$.

Since $n$ is arbitrary, any $r$-dense subset must be infinite for $r \leq 1$.

### Conclusion

A finite $r$-dense subset of the unit ball of $C([0,1])$ exists if and only if $r > 1$.
